items.title: A black hole as light as 40 tons can exist inside a star if dark matter helps
items.summary: In 1974, Stephen Hawking made a prediction that transformed our understanding of black holes. Black holes, he showed, are not truly black: They slowly lose energy through a quantum process now known as Hawking radiation. The lighter the black hole, the faster it evaporates.

items.title: Tree species diversity protects forests from climate extremes, study finds
items.summary: New research has found that tree species diversity can play a crucial role in protecting forests from the growing threat of extreme climate events. items.title: Scientists discover how narwhals grow nature's only straight tusk
items.summary: Narwhals have nature's only straight tusk, a single tooth up to three meters (10 feet) long, so strange they were sold as magical unicorn horns during the Middle Ages.

items.title: Some disagreement makes groups more trustworthy, mathematical framework finds
items.summary: When humans are making decisions, they are known not to rely solely on their own considerations and the evidence available to them. Past behavioral science and psychology studies have shown that people are often also influenced by the choices and opinions of others.

items.title: Lakes aren't just storing water—they're changing the carbon cycle
items.summary: Lakes may look like picturesque stopping points along a river or stream, but they can have a big influence on what happens to carbon as it moves through a landscape. items.title: Ocean indicators NOAA scientists are tracking for El Niño's arrival on the West Coast
items.summary: Has El Niño reached the West Coast? You might think it has. After all, the ocean off Southern and Central California is unusually warm. items.title: Late Roman decrees uncover military system behind amphitheater animal spectacles
items.summary: A study on Roman law by the Carlos III University of Madrid analyzes the regulations and complex imperial logistics governing the capture, transport and safety of animals used in spectacles in the Roman Empire—which were far more popular than gladiatorial combat.

items.title: New method predicts where massive earthquakes will strike
items.summary: UC Riverside scientists have developed a way to identify where Earth's biggest earthquakes are most likely to occur, offering a powerful new tool for improving disaster preparation in some of the most dangerous seismic regions.

items.title: How haze from Indonesian fires impacts Southeast Asia
items.summary: Thick smog has blanketed parts of Indonesia as the vast archipelago battles fires that have burned large swaths of Borneo and Sumatra for weeks.

items.title: Indonesia rescues second orangutan mother and baby from wildfire
items.summary: An orangutan mother and her baby, threatened by wildfires encroaching on their habitat in Indonesia, were rescued earlier this week, authorities said in a statement Saturday.

items.title: Spacecraft bound for Mercury begins 'tricky' arrival
items.summary: After an eight-year journey, a spacecraft carrying European and Japanese probes began the monthslong, high-risk approach to Mercury on Thursday to study the sun-scorched planet.

items.title: Levitated magnet opens new frontier in search for ultraheavy dark matter
items.summary: Rice University researchers have used a magnetically levitated particle to search for ultraheavy dark matter, extending the hunt for some of the heaviest possible forms of the invisible matter thought to hold galaxies together. Led by Christopher Tunnell, associate professor of physics and astronomy

items.title: AI could undermine managers' judgment unless used carefully, study warns
items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) has become a routine part of working life, but overreliance on the technology may erode managers' ability to build moral insights, contextual understanding and know-how to get a job done, according to a new study from the University of Bath.

items.title: Life uses 4 DNA letters. Scientists just made 8 work
items.summary: Researchers at UC San Diego have demonstrated that a key cellular enzyme can accurately read an eight-letter genetic alphabet, doubling the four letters used by all known life on Earth. items.title: Study reveals pupils most at risk of school suspension and what may help them
items.summary: School suspensions are associated with a complex combination of socioeconomic disadvantage, special educational needs, peer relationships and students' experiences of school, according to new research from The University of Manchester.

items.title: Deadly floods of 2021—Researchers identify gaps in hazard mapping
items.summary: The catastrophic flooding in July 2021 claimed the lives of more than 200 people in Germany and Belgium. items.title: Scientists overturn a theory about this shark’s strange head
items.summary: Scientists have overturned a leading explanation for why male and female bonnethead sharks have differently shaped heads. Instead of males developing a pointed snout at maturity, both sexes actually begin with more pointed heads that become rounder with age, particularly in females.

items.title: Researchers tune into Arctic under-ice sounds and test through-ice communication
items.summary: Beneath the Arctic Ocean is an orchestra featuring natural and human composers, from cracking sea ice and whistling beluga whales to humming shipping-vessel engines. items.title: A new type of LED light could bring significant efficiency gains
items.summary: Researchers at Lund University have developed a new type of light-emitting diode based on thin, branched nanowires that could offer significantly higher efficiency and lower production costs than current technology. By controlling where in the structure the light is generated, the researchers have r

items.title: Harvard scientists turn knitting into shape-shifting smart fabric
items.summary: Harvard researchers have transformed ordinary knitting into a platform for creating fabrics that can snap between different shapes and perform useful functions. items.title: In ant nervous systems, gene expression may drive rescue behavior
items.summary: Why do some ants help nestmates in distress while others don't? A research team from Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) and Tel Aviv University addressed this question in a new study. items.title: Magic-angle graphene provides evidence for unconventional superconductivity
items.summary: Researchers have completely suppressed superconductivity in magic-angle graphene by screening interactions between electrons, helping resolve a long-running debate about the origin of the phenomenon.

items.title: New AI tool maps the hidden universe of small molecules
items.summary: The human body and its gut microbiome produce thousands of small molecules that shape how the body functions—influencing immunity, metabolism and more. Identifying what those molecules actually are has been one of the biomedical sciences' most persistent bottlenecks. More than 80% of compounds

items.title: Shoreline scavenger shows biological effects after eating plastic foam
items.summary: In a paper published in the journal Marine Pollution Bulletin, researchers at Kyushu University report on what happens when wharf roaches, a common shoreline scavenger, eat expanded polystyrene (EPS). items.title: Do games make children more attentive or more distractible?
items.summary: A study of preschool children found that brief digital or traditional gameplay improved performance on tasks requiring quick responses but reduced performance on tasks demanding greater concentration and self-control.

items.title: Periodical cicadas may be doomed to extinction
items.summary: Every 13 or 17 years, swarms of cicadas emerge from the ground, their black bodies, orange-tinged wings and ruby-red eyes enveloping trees and forests. It is a biological marvel unique in the insect world, and when it happens, it is impossible not to notice.

items.title: AI helps reveal the immersive sensory experiences of ancient Etruscan tombs
items.summary: The Etruscan painted tombs in Tarquinia, Italy, date to the first millennium BCE and are known for their vivid scenes of music, feasting, processions and the afterlife. items.title: Before mixing starts, initial catalyst structure governs fuel-cell ink dispersion
items.summary: Researchers from Kanazawa University, the University of Tokyo and HORIBA, Ltd. have shown that the initial state of platinum-on-carbon (Pt/C) catalyst particles before they are mixed with an ionomer strongly influences how a polymer electrolyte fuel cell (PEFC) catalyst ink subsequently develops. items.title: Evidence-based approach shows de-escalation is a learnable police skill
items.summary: A three-year research collaboration between Florida State University's College of Criminology and Criminal Justice and the Leon County Sheriff's Office (LCSO) has produced one of the most comprehensive real-world studies on police de-escalation to date.

items.title: How Mercury formed its graphite crust and core
items.summary: As the BepiColombo mission prepares to enter the final phase of its journey to Mercury, a series of studies conducted by researchers at the University of Liège and KU Leuven sheds new light on the early stages of the evolution of the planet closest to the sun. items.title: NASA Ames Fire Department Aircraft Firefighting Training
items.summary: The fire department at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley will perform training on the Moffett Federal Airfield beginning Tuesday, Sept. 8 through Friday, Sept. 11. The training will involve the use of a propane-fueled aircraft fire simulator and be conducted from 8 a.m. to 8

items.title: El Niño set to bring warmer spring to NZ and Australia
items.summary: El Niño is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with major impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns and associated risks of floods, drought and extreme heat, according to a new update from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

items.title: Embedded platinum channels bring nanoscale spin-based thermoelectric conversion to bulk materials
items.summary: A joint research team from NIMS and the University of Tokyo has developed a new composite in which three-dimensional nano-interfaces are distributed throughout the material by coating the surfaces of magnetic-insulator powders with a metal and sintering them. Using this structure, the team succeeded

items.title: Food and water stations for wild birds are contributing to spread of deadly diseases, study finds
items.summary: Feeding stations providing food and water for wild birds are contributing to the spread of disease-causing parasites among farmland birds, researchers have said, with birds three times more likely to catch a parasite from these resources.

items.title: Students with lower grades earn degrees more often when they belong to an academic major's majority group
items.summary: Despite efforts to encourage broader participation, women earn about 25% of undergraduate engineering degrees and 18% of undergraduate computer science degrees—and men remain a small minority among people earning nursing and education degrees.

items.title: Same-sex marriages surged before Bolsonaro took office, Brazil data reveal
items.summary: A new study has shown that the election of Jair Bolsonaro, known for his homophobic views, as president of Brazil in 2018 caused a temporary surge in the number of same-sex marriages. The increase was particularly high in Brazilian municipalities where a large number of voters had previously voted f

items.title: Virus-like particles enable gene activity tracking over time in the same cells
items.summary: In recent years, scientists have developed methods to measure a cell's transcriptome, or all the RNA produced by a cell, to study the cell's identity and genetic activity. However, these methods rely on killing the cell to access the bits of RNA within and offer only a one-time snapshot.

items.title: Sound waves and water droplets transform paper waste into higher-value chemical compound
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have developed a fast, simple way to turn lignin, a plentiful plant-based byproduct of the papermaking industry, into potentially more valuable renewable chemicals.

items.title: Underlying mechanism of Atg2-mediated lipid transfer in autophagy identified
items.summary: Autophagy is an intracellular degradation mechanism in eukaryotes. The autophagosome, which encloses damaged or excess cellular material for degradation, is constructed from lipids supplied by the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) via the lipid transfer protein Atg2.

items.title: Particle shape and size predict asteroid strength, revealing Bennu's surface is 50 times weaker than ground coffee
items.summary: In a new Nature Communications study, researchers developed a universal scaling framework for the strength of granular asteroids, showing that their tensile strength can be predicted from the size and shape of their constituent particles.

items.title: From pets to zoos: How students perceive animal husbandry
items.summary: Animals fulfill a wide range of roles in human society. They provide food, contribute to scientific research, live alongside people as companion animals, and play important roles in education, conservation, research and public engagement through zoos.

items.title: Want a solution to plastic pollution? Scientists urge UN to require global reporting
items.summary: Plastic is a wonder material that has molded itself to fit a wide variety of applications. But it comes with a host of drawbacks that aren't fully considered. That's why the United Nations has convened to hammer out a treaty to address plastic pollution.

items.title: Archaea as 'flexitarians': Ammonia-oxidizing microbes also feed on amino acids
items.summary: Symbiotic ammonia-oxidizing archaea in marine sponges are not strict specialists but true "flexitarians." items.title: Mixed grazing, controlled burns and collaboration can curb Mediterranean wildfire risks
items.summary: Wildfires in the Mediterranean region are becoming drastically more intense. The recent major fires in France, Spain and Greece show that firefighting efforts are reaching their limits.

items.title: Turbulent times for star formation in Stephan's Quintet
items.summary: Star formation in galaxies is closely linked to molecular gas. In the distant past, when galaxy interactions were more common, these encounters compressed molecular gas, causing dense clouds to collapse under their own gravity and form new stars.

items.title: Mosque workshops help Muslim women discuss reproductive health in NSW
items.summary: Governments across Australia have pledged hundreds of millions of dollars toward women's health services in recent months and years—but having more health services won't help if people don't know they're available or how to access them.

items.title: 'Hidden order in disorder' makes nanodevices easier to design
items.summary: Augmented reality (AR) glasses, lenses thinner than a human hair, and holograms floating above your fingertips may sound like technologies from science fiction. At the heart of these emerging technologies, however, lies a nanoscale optical device known as a "metasurface."
